scene.testo: Sixteen. That is how many sunrises and sunsets an astronaut sees every single day. Sixteen. The station circles Earth every ninety minutes. So when do you sleep? And why aren't you terrified to close your eyes up there?

Imagine you are floating at 250 miles above Earth. It is bedtime. Your body zooms along at 17,500 mph. Below you, the sun just dropped behind the planet. Again. You zip up a sleeping bag and tie yourself to a wall.

No bed. No pillow. No ceiling above you and no floor beneath you. Just a bag clipped to a wall, and a body that has no idea which way is up. Most people would panic. Astronauts drift off. Here is why.

First, the problem. Your brain runs on a clock that is about twenty-four hours long. It expects one sunrise and one sunset. Outside the station window, the sun rises and sets about every forty-five minutes. Your body gets completely confused.

Astronauts say the light show is stunning. It is also a sleep thief. Imagine trying to nap while a window flashes gold, then black, then gold again. Every forty-five minutes. All night. So the crew does something simple.

They run the station on a clock people can live with. The International Space Station keeps Greenwich Mean Time. That is the time in London. Whether the crew is flying over Texas or Tokyo, the schedule says the same thing.
Wake up around 6 AM. Work all day. Lights out around 9:30 PM. That is roughly what NASA schedules for the crew. Eight and a half hours are set aside for sleep. The sun outside does not get a vote.

Now, the place you actually sleep. On the American side of the station, each astronaut gets a small private cabin. NASA describes them as about the size of a phone booth. Roughly the width of a closet. And it is yours.
scene.capitolo: A Cabin Like a Phone Booth

scene.testo: Inside is a sleeping bag fastened to the wall. A laptop. A few photos from home. Some clothes in a pocket. The walls are padded, and there is a small light you can switch off. It is cozy. Tiny, but cozy.

Now picture the bag. It is not lying flat. It is tied to the wall, vertical or sideways, it makes no difference. Up there, there is no down. Astronauts have said they sleep fine pointing in any direction.

Here is a detail that surprises people. If you did not strap in, you would float. Overnight, you might drift across the module. Bump a wall. Wake up with your face against a fan. That is why the bag is tied.

And fans matter. In space, warm air does not rise. There is no up for it to rise toward. Your own exhaled breath can hang around your face in a bubble. That bubble is carbon dioxide. Breathing it is a real danger.

So the station runs air fans around the clock. Astronauts have talked about the constant hum. It keeps fresh air moving past your face while you sleep. Without it, you could wake up with a headache, or worse.

Which brings us to the big question. Why aren't they afraid? You are asleep in a metal tube. Outside is a vacuum. The temperature swings between roughly minus 250 and plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. Why doesn't that keep them awake?

Answer number one: training. Astronauts spend years preparing. Before launch, they practice emergencies again and again. Fire. Pressure leaks. Toxic air. They drill each scenario until their hands move without thinking.

They train underwater in a giant pool at NASA in Houston. They rehearse in full-size mockups of the station. Fear shrinks when you have practiced the worst case a hundred times. It is the same reason pilots stay calm.

Answer number two: alarms. The station has smoke detectors and sensors for pressure and air quality. If something goes wrong, an alarm sounds, loud enough to wake anyone. You are not the only thing watching the station.

Answer number three: Mission Control. Even while the crew sleeps, teams of flight controllers work on the ground. They watch the station's data around the clock, in shifts. If something looks wrong, they can call the crew.

Think of it like a night nurse on a hospital ward. You sleep. Somebody else watches the monitors. The Houston control room, along with partner centers in Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada, never fully goes dark.

Answer number four: the walls. The station's outer shell is not paper thin. It carries layers of shielding against tiny bits of space debris. Those bits can travel at many thousands of miles per hour. The shielding is designed for them.

That said, we should be honest. Risk is real. NASA tracks debris constantly. Sometimes the station has to move out of the way. It is not zero risk. Astronauts know that. They accept it, the way a test pilot does.

In fact, astronauts have shared something interesting in interviews. The calm is real. Many describe feeling safer up there than people expect. They trust the machine, the crew, and the team in Houston. Trust is the secret.

Now let's talk about something stranger. Does sleep feel normal up there? Not exactly. Astronauts report lighter sleep. Some wake often. Studies of crews have found they average less than the eight hours scheduled. Closer to six.

Why? Noise, for one. The station is never quiet. Pumps, fans, and equipment run nonstop. Light is another reason. Even in a dark cabin, small lights glow. And the work schedule is demanding. Tired is normal up there.

Some astronauts use eye masks and earplugs. Some listen to music. Some say the hum becomes a lullaby after a few weeks. Humans adapt. Your brain decides the noise is safe, and it stops paying attention.

Then there is the feeling of weightlessness itself. On Earth, your bed pushes back against you. Pressure points ache and you roll over. In orbit, nothing pushes. Astronauts often describe it as floating on a cloud.
Some report that their arms drift up while they sleep. Arms float out in front of you like a sleepwalker. It looks funny, and it is harmless. It is just what a relaxed body does when gravity is gone.

And there is the light that never lets go. Every sunrise outside can sneak through the window. Many crew cabins have no window at all, which helps. In the open modules, crews sometimes cover windows with shades to fake night.

Here is a strange effect astronauts have reported. Some see flashes of light with their eyes closed. Tiny streaks, like sparks. Scientists link these to cosmic rays, high-energy particles passing through the eye. Not everyone sees them.

Cosmic rays are particles that zip through space at tremendous speed. Out here, Earth's magnetic field shields us. Up at 250 miles, the shield is thinner. Not gone, but thinner. So particles sometimes reach the crew.

The station does protect the crew from most radiation. Some areas are better shielded than others. Crews have sometimes picked the best-protected spots to sleep. Researchers study this closely, because longer trips to Mars will face stronger radiation.

Now compare it to your night. You sleep under a roof, on a mattress, in one steady time zone. One sunset. One sunrise. Gravity holds you down. Up there, nothing holds you but a strap. And still, they sleep.

Here is a size comparison. The station is about as long as a football field, counting its solar arrays. Roughly 357 feet across. Yet the living space inside is more like a large house. And the crew sleeps in tiny cabins.
scene.q: space station solar arrays full view

scene.testo: Six or seven people live on board at a time. Imagine sharing a house with six coworkers, for six months, hundreds of miles from the nearest neighbor. Sleep is the one moment each person gets some privacy.

And yes, crews bond. They eat dinner together. They watch movies together. Many astronauts say the crew becomes like family. That matters for sleep, because you rest easier knowing people you trust are awake nearby.

Now, what about the early days? Back in the Apollo era, sleeping was rougher. On the way to the Moon, crews slept in the spacecraft, in small hammocks or in couches. Space was tight, and the cabins were noisy.

On the Moon itself, Apollo crews slept inside the lunar module, which was cramped. Astronauts have described hanging hammocks across the cabin. They also noted the cold, and the pounding noise from the equipment.

Yet those men slept. They trusted their training and their ground teams, just like crews today. They also had tremendous adrenaline. Some reported lying awake in wonder, knowing the Moon sat just outside the thin wall.

Fast forward to long stays. Skylab, in the 1970s, gave crews private sleeping compartments. Astronauts liked them. They were quiet, dark, and roomy compared to earlier craft. The idea of a bedroom in space was born.
Today, a station stay lasts about six months. Some astronauts have stayed close to a year. That is hundreds of nights in a bag on a wall. Sleep is not a luxury up there. It is part of the mission.

NASA studies sleep closely. Crews wear monitors and keep logs. Doctors want to know how rest changes in orbit, because tired astronauts make mistakes. Better sleep means a safer station and a stronger path to Mars.

Some stations have also tested special lighting. Bulbs that shift color through the day. Bluer in the morning, warmer at night. The goal is to trick your body clock into thinking there is a normal sunset. It helps.

So why aren't astronauts afraid to sleep in space? Because training, alarms, shielding, and a team in Houston stand guard. And because humans adapt. Fear fades when you trust the system watching over you.

Now the most surprising detail. Astronauts often say that falling asleep up there is the easy part. The hard part is waking up. Because for a moment, drifting in the dark, you forget where you are. Then you remember.

You open your eyes, and a sunrise is already pouring through the window. Earth is glowing blue below you. Sixteen sunrises a day, and you are floating above all of them. That is what they sleep next to.

descrizione:
Why aren't astronauts afraid to sleep in space? On the International Space Station, the sun rises and sets about sixteen times a day, the crew sleeps in bags tied to the wall, and the station moves at 17,500 mph, 250 miles above Earth. This Orbital Days documentary explains how astronauts sleep in orbit, what their cabins look like, how training, alarms and Mission Control keep them safe, and why sleep in space feels so different from sleep at home.

We walk through a real night on the ISS: the sleeping bag, the fans, the light, the noise, the cosmic ray flashes some crews report, and how the station's schedule fools the body clock. We also compare it with Apollo and Skylab nights and with your own bedroom.

All facts come from NASA, ESA and astronauts' own accounts. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more questions about life in space.
